BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: Light valley rain and mountain snow will continue through Monday morning, with minimal accumulations anticipated. A ridge of high pressure will build back into the region by late Monday, bringing a short-lived warming and drying trend.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Valley rain and mountain snow will taper off by the late morning with the highest snow totals southwest of the Snake River Valley.
- Breezy northwesterly winds up to 35 mph will continue in the Baker Valley and Magic Valley through the evening.
- A generally cool and wet pattern will continue through next week, with brief dry periods on Saturday and next Tuesday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: A low pressure system is moving over the region this morning, bringing widespread precipitation, low stratus, and breezy winds. Snow is falling generally above 3500-4000 ft MSL as the low center is squarely over the Owyhee Mountains this morning. Cooler air is funneling down the Baker/Treasure Valleys as the low moves east, but uncertainty remains on whether warm air aloft will keep rain the predominant precipitation type in the Boise metro area. Ensemble max from high resolution models show 1.4 inches of snow in Boise, but with warm air still firmly in place, the likelihood of this is very low (<10% chance). Current temperatures at 3am are right at 39F at Treasure Valley sites, but the latest forecast lowers surface temperatures down to 32-35F. This paired with dewpoints above freezing will likely keep rain the predominant precipitation type. Current forecast favors the warmer solution for the Treasure Valley, with snow levels staying generally above 3500-4000 ft MSL. Higher elevations south and west of the Snake River Valley will see impactful snow accumulations, with 2-4 inches of snow by late morning. This is already creating difficult travel conditions along Highway 51 and 95, as evidenced by webcams showing snowfall and breezy winds at Ion Summit. A winter weather advisory is in effect until 11AM MST for Malheur County, the Owyhee Mountains, and the western portion of the Southern Highlands. Ridgetops above about 7000 ft in the Owyhees, Steens, and near the ID-NV border will see an additional 6-10 inches of snow by late morning. This low pressure system will move east by the early afternoon, leaving cooler and breezy conditions in its wake. Westerly winds will be strongest in the Magic Valley and in southern Baker County, with gusts up to 35 mph during the afternoon.

High pressure will build in behind the low passage this afternoon, with a few lingering terrain forced showers over the region. Dry and cold conditions will linger through Saturday, with fog forming in higher terrain and in sheltered valleys late Friday night. A shortwave trough will move through the region late Sunday, bringing another quick hit of valley rain and mountain snow. Colder temperatures overnight paired with lingering precipitation will bring another chance for a valley rain-snow mix on Sunday morning before sunrise. This unsettled pattern will keep temperatures slightly below normal, with overnight lows staying below freezing throughout the region starting tomorrow night.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Light valley rain and mountain snow will continue through Monday morning, with minimal accumulations anticipated. A ridge of high pressure will build back into the region by late Monday, bringing a short-lived warming and drying trend. A deep upper level low and associated atmospheric river will begin to move towards the PacNW coast on Wednesday, eventually splitting and staying offshore. Remnant moisture from this system will be advected into the region thanks to southwest flow aloft, bringing more valley rain and mountain snow by midweek. Precipitation will mainly be in southeast Oregon and over higher terrain in southwest Idaho. Model agreement diverges significantly after Thursday, primarily on the position of an upper level low just west of Vancouver Island and the strength of a ridge of high pressure over the West Coast. The current long term forecast favors the warmer and drier scenario, which would keep the ridge of high pressure stronger and over the Intermountain West.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: Brief upper-level ridging is expected to return by Saturday night that will bring drier conditions back to Colorado, but won't have much impact on the cooler temperatures.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Next storm system arrives today, bringing chances for light mountain snow through Saturday.
- Gusty winds and elevated fire weather conditions this afternoon across most of the Front Range foothills and plains.
- Cooler pattern emerges this weekend into next week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Our next approaching storm system is visible on satellite imagery moving across the Great Basin tonight. Current METAR observations show snow showers have begun to move into the northern mountains, where southwesterly flow will favor the Park Range. 3-6 inches are forecast between today and Saturday, with locally higher amounts possible at the highest elevations. As this shortwave approaches, southwesterly flow will steadily increase as the night progresses and an 80-90kt 500mb jet moves over Colorado. While there will be enough moisture for light mountain snow showers today, the main weather impacts will be with gusty winds and elevated to near- critical fire weather conditions developing across portions of the plains and Palmer Divide this afternoon. Gusty southwesterly winds mixed with above-normal temperatures are expected to drop relative humidity (RH) values down to 17%-22% across the plains, where 30-40mph winds are expected to develop by late morning. There isn't expected to be enough of an overlap with the lowest RH and gusty winds to warrant any fire weather highlights, but elevated fire weather conditions can be expected across much of the lower elevations this afternoon. Additionally, with the jet overhead, expect strong winds gusting up to 65-70mph at times over our high mountain peaks, but gusts should generally be 40-50mph over the mountains, with some 30-40mph gusts making their way down the lee of the Front Range. A cold front is expected to slide across the forecast area later this afternoon and evening that will shift surface winds to the northwest, advecting a much colder airmass into Colorado.

With colder temperatures expected behind the front, snow levels will drop overnight, and we may see some snow flurries across the lower elevations by Saturday morning when temperatures will drop below freezing, and QG forcing is greatest as the shortwave passes just to our south. Unfortunately, this once robust looking system just won't have enough juice to bring any accumulating snowfall to our lower elevations, but we may see a few tenths in our high mountain valleys, southern foothills, and along the Palmer Divide when all is said and done. Saturday's afternoon high temperatures will be roughly 5 to 10 degrees below seasonal values across the forecast area, with 30s and 40s forecasted for the plains, and 30s for the mountain valleys.

Brief upper-level ridging is expected to return by Saturday night that will bring drier conditions back to Colorado, but won't have much impact on the cooler temperatures. Afternoon high temps will finally start to resemble November normals, with the plains actually looking to be a few degrees below seasonal values through at least the middle of next week. Uncertainties remain with the strength and track of our next potential shortwave (Monday?), but it's not looking like any significant precipitation will be possible outside of a few waves of light mountain snowfall through the forecast period.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Tuesday will remain chilly behind the departing storm system, but we should see more sunshine.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Locally heavy snow showers continue through Friday morning mainly in Carbon County.
- Isolated to scattered light snow shower activity will remain possible in Carbon, Albany, and Converse Counties through Saturday.
- Another round of strong, gusty winds is expected mid morning through the evening Friday.
- Elevated fire weather conditions are expected over the High Plains Friday.
- Expect chillier temperatures this weekend into early next week with a few additional chances for light, spotty snow showers.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: A large, but messy and disorganized storm system is driving our weather this morning, and will be responsible for generally unsettled weather over the area for the next 48 hours or so. While the primary upper level low is still back over the Great Basin, a secondary shortwave leads the primary trough along an area of deep, moist southwest flow encroaching into Carbon County. Orographic ascent combined with convective instability are supporting numerous locally heavy snow showers over the area. Mesoanalysis indicates around 100 to 300 J/kg MUCAPE this morning. This was enough to get some thundersnow going around Rawlins earlier this morning! SWE rates have been fairly impressive under the heavier bands, but the snow has not been steady. SNOTELs in the Sierra Madre have observed 0.2" SWE per hour, while Rawlins picked up 0.1" in about a half hour. This generally suggests snowfall rates maximizing around 2" per hour. A Winter Weather Advisory was issued for the Sierra Madre range where orographic lift has been maintaining more consistent snowfall above 8000 ft or so. For the rest of Carbon county, the spotty nature of the showers reduces confidence in exactly where more notable snow accumulations will occur. Therefore, a Special Weather Statement for a widespread 1-3" of snow was issued for the lower elevations of Carbon county. Snow showers will also spill into portions of Albany and Converse counties this morning. One area we will be watching this morning is the northern part of the county around Muddy Gap east towards the edge of the Shirley Basin. Radar returns have shown some training snow shower activity in this area, which could lead to accumulations on the higher end of the range. Drier air is expected to move into the area between about 8AM and noon. This will reduce snow shower coverage and snowfall rates significantly through the rest of the day afterwards, but don't expect the radar to completely clear. Further east, the surface environment has reached saturation around Scotts Bluff, Box Butte, and Morrill counties, supporting some locally dense fog. A Dense Fog Advisory was issued through 9AM, but satellite trends are showing that this may be already eroding as winds turn westerly over the High Plains.

Once drier air moves into the area later this morning, we will also see winds aloft increasing quickly. West-southwest winds will overspread the area by midday, leading to another windy day. For most, gusts will be in the 40 to 55 mph range, but the possibility remains for locally higher gusts in the typical wind prone areas. This was a pretty tricky wind forecast, and thus lower confidence than usual. Most of our usual height/pressure gradient parameters are below what we would want to see for high winds and the potential for mountain wave breaking looks limited due to a fairly unstable lower atmosphere. On the other hand, winds aloft around 45 to 55 knots may be present in a deep, well-mixed boundary layer. High resolution models are also resolving stronger briefly stronger surface wind gusts exceeding high wind criteria. In-house guidance has nudged slightly upward today, with probabilities around 50% for the southern Laramie range and foothills, 40% near Bordeaux, and 70% for northern Platte county (between Wheatland and Glendo). The Arlington/Elk Mountain area remains a little lower, around 30%. So all together, this is extremely marginal, but decided to issue a High Wind Warning for the typical wind prone areas. Gusts have a lower ceiling today, and should not be as consistent as they were with Wednesday's event. Winds will also produce elevated fire weather conditions over much of the High Plains, though relative humidity is expected to stay above critical thresholds. Winds will continue along and west of the Laramie range overnight, but should become spottier to the east.

A weak cold front will pass through the plains, getting Saturday off to a chilly start as widely scattered snow shower activity continues over our northern and western areas. Look for a breezy and chilly day across much of the area. A reinforcing cold front will push through Saturday afternoon, which should set up Sunday with the coldest morning of the season so far.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: The axis of the primary upper level trough will pass through the area Sunday morning, bringing an end to the unsettled weather pattern. Lingering snow showers should depart the area before dawn Sunday morning, though the area will remain colder than seasonal averages as the chilly surface high lingers over the area. Very weak transient ridging will try to build in Monday, so we should warm up a few degrees over Sunday's highs as the surface stationary front retreats slightly to the northeast away from the terrain. The next Pacific trough will approach from the west, and chances for snow showers return to the mountains during the daytime hours Monday. This system has once again trended towards a disorganized sprawling system with messy forcing for lift. The mountains may manage to pick up another round of light snow but even the orographic lift looks less impressive with this system. Outside of the mountains, about 50% of ensembles show a dusting to an inch of snow falling, while the others remain completely dry. Low end PoPs continue Monday night, but the odds of notable snowfall are quite low.

Tuesday will remain chilly behind the departing storm system, but we should see more sunshine. More organized ridging is expected to start to build in on Wednesday, pushing temperatures back to near or slightly above seasonal averages for the latter part of the work week. Another system may traverse across the region Wednesday into Thursday (Thanksgiving), but this again looks weak, disorganized, and moisture-starved. For now, low end PoPs are present in the mountains but the probability is too low to include a mention of snow for the plains and valleys.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: As this system moves on out of the region, look for generally mild weather with temperatures running near normal. The models are struggling in this transition period between summer and winter, and can't seem to agree on much.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Measurable snowfall is expected today into Saturday for the Colorado mountains, with some high valleys also seeing light accumulations.
- Temperatures will trend downward for the weekend, with most desert valleys seeing their first freezing temperatures of the year.
- Fast moving storms are possible through much of Thanksgiving week. Stay tuned for updates to timing and impacts as they become available.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Models are in fair agreement with satellite imagery, but seem to be struggling with the mesoscale features like the low vortex tracking to the northeast across Wyoming. This low is dragging the cold front, currently over the Park Range extending to the southwest to Grand Mesa and the Uncompahgre Plateau, to the east across eastern Utah and Western Colorado. This Front is driving wind gust over 40 mph and a band of showers ahead of it with rain below about 9,000 feet. Though these showers were heavier earlier this morning, they are now mostly light showers with brief periods of moderate rain and snow as drier air moves in to the region. Look for this boundary to push on through the region though the afternoon with gusty southwest winds ahead of the front shifting to the northwest and dropping off behind the front.

As this system moves on out of the region, look for generally mild weather with temperatures running near normal. The models are struggling in this transition period between summer and winter, and can't seem to agree on much. They don't see any deep low pressure systems dropping south as we had for the last month or so that brought the heavy rains and flooding across the region, but more an extended period of unsettled weather with fast moving disturbances moving through every few days. The first of these will move through early next week with a second system in the mid-week time frame and a third later in the week into the weekend. Currently there is no significant moisture with any of these systems and we don't anticipate any weather headlines, but there is little confidence in the forecast at this time, so stay tuned for updates as we go into next week. If you plan to travel through the mountains over Thanksgiving, be prepared for possible periods of icy or snowy roads over the higher mountain passes. Plan to leave early to allow extra travel time so you can arrive at your destination safely.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Dry and cool weather will continue for mid week under another transient upper ridge.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Potential for high winds along the east slopes of the southern Sangre De Cristo mountains and western Huerfano county today, otherwise warm and windy for most of the lower elevations.
- Windy with rounds of light mountain snows across the Continental Divide, spreading into the southeast mountains on Saturday.
- Cooler Saturday with a few light showers possible across the southeast plains.
- Below normal temperatures for Sunday into next week with fast moving systems bringing opportunities for light showers Monday and Thursday, mainly mountains.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Winds have been increasing across the mountains with gusts in the 40 to 55 mph range across the higher mountains and along the lee slopes of the southeast mountains. Snow has spread into the eastern San Juans and portions of the Sawatch range as southwest flow ahead of the approaching western U.S. upper low advects moisture into the region.

Winds will continue to increase overnight, peaking in intensity later this morning as the upper jet translates overhead and energy within southwest flow ejects from southwest to northeast across CO. While winds will increase into the 50-65 mph range across most of the mountains, the best chance for high winds still looks targeted across the southern Sangres and Huerfano county this morning. Cross-sections/soundings off RRFS show a less defined mountain top stable layer with more laminar flow instead of the weak reverse shear seen in runs from 24 hours ago. Probabilities of winds exceeding high wind criteria (75 mph mountains, 58 mph lower elevations) have come down a bit as well, though odds are still around 50-70% range off REFS (less off NBM). HRRR still shows spotty high winds occuring in the 15z-20z window, though this may be due more to mixing/downward forcing behind the embedded wave, rather than mountain wave induced high winds. Still think spotty areas could see some brief damaging gusts spreading into the southern I-25 corridor of Huerfano county, so will maintain high wind warnings. Otherwise, downsloping will result in another warm and windy day across the lower elevations while the Continental Divide continues to pick up rounds of light wind driven snow across the higher areas. Elevated fire weather conditions will be possible along the adjacent plains today, though minimum humidity values will stay above critical thresholds and no fire weather highlights are anticipated.

Snow decreases along the Continental Divide this afternoon, but increases again tonight as the main upper trough approaches out west. The Continental Divide will see another 1-2 inches of wind driven snow overnight, with the heaviest falling across the eastern San Juans. A cold front will sag southward into the southeast plains overnight, though moisture will be lacking, and most of the area will remain dry.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Showers will spread eastward on Saturday as the upper trough moves across southern CO through the day. The front will back door into the southeast plains bringing cooler temperatures to the plains. Moisture appears scant behind the front, but some showers may spill off into the adjacent I-25 corridor and southern portions of the plains during the afternoon as the upper forcing moves through. Overall, any precipitation will be light with a dusting to up to an inch of snow possible across the southeast mountains, and some spotty light precipitation amounts possible across the adjacent plains.

Dry weather returns for Saturday night into Sunday, and temperatures Sunday morning will dip into the teens and single digits for the mountains/valley locations under clear skies. The plains will see lows in the 20s.
Sunday will remain dry and cool under shortwave ridging.

Another fast moving system will move across CO on Monday-Monday night. Similar to the previous system, some wind driven snow will spread into the mountains, and depending on the amplitude of the weakening trough as it moves across the plains, we could see some showers spill over into the southeast plains. Overall, any precipitation will be brief and light.

Dry and cool weather will continue for mid week under another transient upper ridge. Yet another system is progged to move through around the Thanksgiving holiday, though it seems more likely to be another open wave producing some light mountain snows according to various ensemble means. Operational GFS appears to be the outlier solution with a closed low dropping into the Desert Southwest on Thursday. Even this solution would keep the majority of the precipitation too far south to affect southern CO. There's been quite a bit of run to run variability over the past couple days with this latter system, keeping the details uncertain. Cool and unsettled weather with light mountain snows seems the most likely scenario for the time being.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: The ridge is expected to track east of the area by late in the weekend, with a relatively active pattern continuing for the West for the upcoming week. There is high confidence in a storm system impacting the area on Monday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - A Pacific Northwest storm system will continue to bring periods of precipitation to northern Utah through this evening, particularly for areas near the Utah/Idaho border. This will bring travel difficulties across the mountains of northern Utah as well as the Wasatch Back. Snow levels are expected to drop to around 4,500 feet by this evening.

- There is a high chance of temperatures near or below freezing for portions of lower Washington county as well as the Virgin River corridor near Zion National Park Saturday morning. Near freezing temperatures are also anticipated Sunday morning.
- Dry conditions are expected over the weekend, with an active pattern continuing into next week as a weaker system impacts Utah and southwest Wyoming Monday.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A broad but weakening Pacific Northwest storm system continues to track across Utah and southwest Wyoming this morning. Precipitation is focused over the area of best cold pool instability over northern Utah, with snow levels near 5,000 feet. Precipitation will continue during the day and into the evening, though coverage will steadily decrease during that time. By this evening, remaining precipitation should be primarily focused from Ogden northward, with some light precipitation continuing near the Utah/Idaho border through early Saturday morning. By late evening, snow levels are expected to drop to all northern Utah valley floors, though precipitation will likely have ended over much of the Wasatch Front by that time, limiting the potential for accumulating snow. Have cancelled the Winter Weather Advisory for the southern mountains as precipitation has ended there, but have kept remaining headlines as is for now.

Behind the exiting trough, high pressure is expected to be the dominant feature over Utah and southwest Wyoming this weekend. With things clearing quickly over southern Utah, temperatures will drop noticeably tonight in an unseasonably cold airmass. This will bring a high chance of below freezing temperatures to areas in the Virgin River corridor near Zion National Park, with a good chance of freezing to near freezing temperatures for portions of lower Washington county as well Saturday morning. Temperatures are expected to creep up a bit Sunday morning, but lows could stay near freezing for those areas. Overall, looking at maxes 5-10F below seasonal normals Saturday and near normal to up to 5F below seasonal normals on Sunday.

The ridge is expected to track east of the area by late in the weekend, with a relatively active pattern continuing for the West for the upcoming week. There is high confidence in a storm system impacting the area on Monday. This will be weaker than the last few systems but is likely to bring accumulating snow to the mountains. There is still significant model spread on some details, however, such as which areas might see the best accumulations. Another system is then expected to follow later in the upcoming week, though details for that system are even murkier.

2660.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Mike Walter
bottom_line: You can trigger avalanches large enough to bury you at upper elevations. You can trigger these slides from the side or bottom of a slope. Steer clear of steep slopes where you encounter wind-stiffened snow or see shooting cracks as you travel. Look for and avoid drifted snow below ridges and on the sides of gullies.
Below treeline conditions are generally safe.

2745.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Jason Konigsberg
bottom_line: Most slopes are safe and lack sufficient coverage for an avalanche. At high elevations, steer clear of isolated patches of firm, drifted snow below ridges or in steep gullies.

3046.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

1736.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

3014.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
bottom_line: Winter has begun to embrace the West Central Mountains of Idaho. 6-12 inches of new snow has fallen between Friday the 13th and Monday the 16th. Another 6-12 inches could stack up by the end of the week. If you're traveling in the mountains this week, watch out for wind slabs 1-2 feet thick above 7,000 feet and pay attention to terrain traps.
We'll update the General Avalanche Information weekly until full-time forecasting operations begin.
hazard_discussion: From 60-degree temperatures to over a foot of new snow, the weather sure has changed quickly over the past week. A cooler and wetter weather pattern has taken shape over our region since Friday the 13th. As of Monday (16th) afternoon, some mountain locations have picked up 6-12 inches of new snow along with southerly winds gusting 20-30 MPH.
Wind Slabs
• Wind slabs could become reactive this week with over a foot of new snow and gusty winds. Wind slabs will be most sensitive just below ridgelines.
• Look for clues of wind-affected snow, such as drifts, dunes, pillows, and freshly built cornices.
• Watch for signs of instability, such as shooting cracks. If you're observing these signs, find another aspect away from wind-drifted snow.
• Strong winds and local terrain features can alter the prevailing wind direction. Pay attention to cross-loading and wind-loading on unsuspecting slopes.
Early Season Conditions
• If you're out hiking or hunting in the mountains this fall, stay tuned to changing weather conditions. Avalanches are most likely during and immediately after a storm.

• Keep in mind the adage, "If there's enough snow to ride, there's enough snow to slide". Even if there's not enough snow to bury you, a small slide over uncovered logs, rocks, and brush would not be a fun way to start the season.
• Stay up to date on mountain weather with our WEATHER tab, where you'll find webcams, weather stations, and weather forecasting tools.
Check Your Winter Gear

• Beacons, shovels, probes, airbags. Run through all your gear and make sure it's functioning properly. Does your transceiver or airbag need any firmware updates? Look for cracks, defects, or corroded batteries. Make it fun with your friends and do a pre-season gear check with your winter travel companions.
Continuing Education
• Check out the Education tab on our website to sign up for avalanche courses this winter (COURSES ).
• Stay tuned to our EVENTS pages for other local happenings with the winter community.
• Interested in attending a snow and avalanche workshop (SAW)? Check out A3's WEBSITE for a list of events.
Observations
• Keep an eye on our observation page HERE

• If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation HERE. Early season observations help forecasters and the public alike. A simple photo and/or weather observation helps paint the picture of where snow is and where it is not.

Yeah, that's right: the Payette Avalanche Center has a new website. Browse around before the snow starts flying. We're also on the Avy App. You can search for "Avy: Avalanche & Weather Info" in your app store on your mobile device.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Dylan Craaybeek
bottom_line: Most slopes are generally safe from avalanches. You might be able to trigger a small avalanche where you encounter stiff, wind-drifted snow on the lee sides of ridgelines or above treeline terrain where blowing snow accumulates.
